claim.why_it_matters: Three sibling headings are transcribed at two different levels - 14.6.2.3.1 at '####' but 14.6.2.3.2 and 14.6.2.3.3 at '##'. In the rendered outline 'Initial state' and 'Last-used state' detach from their parent 14.6.2.3 entirely and become peers of clause 14.6. These are the normative definitions of when static/automatic/initial data is reset, so an outline-driven lookup landing in the wrong subtree is a real navigation hazard.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED. Nothing is missing and no normative content differs; the claim is a markdown-formatting observation misfiled as 'missing-heading', and the pattern it points at is page-break furniture that is global to the transcription rather than a defect on page 568. (1) The headings are PRESENT and CORRECT. The rendered PDF (E:/Temp/specrecon/v568/spec_p568.png, printed folio 538) shows exactly two bold clause headings: '14.6.2.3.2 Initial state' and '14.6.2.3.3 Last-used state'. specs/ISO_COBOL.md carries both, verbatim, with the correct clause numbers and titles, at lines 23759 and 23790, each preceded by its own resolvable anchor (, ). The clause number - the authoritative depth signal, and the key any spec lookup actually uses - is fully preserved in both the heading text and the anchor id. (2) The page body is complete. Full sentence-by-sentence comparison of the render against E:/Temp/specrecon/v568/page-568.md found zero omissions: the two lead-in paragraphs, the 3-item 'Static data is placed in the initial state' list, the 'When data ... is placed in the initial state' lead-in, all 7 numbered steps (INITIALIZE/OPTIONS fill character; VALUE clause 13.18.63; internal file connectors; screen item attributes; based-item address null; dynamic-capacity table minimum capacity + INITIALIZED keyword; dynamic-length item length zero), the 'Before data is placed in the initial state ... 12.3.6, OBJECT-COMPUTER paragraph' paragraph, and the whole 14.6.2.3.3 body. Meaning is unchanged in every respect. (3) The level difference is page-break furniture, and it is SYSTEMIC, not local. The transcription assigns heading levels PAGE-LOCALLY: the first clause heading on a page is emitted at '##' whatever its true depth, and deeper subclauses on that same page nest relative to it. Verified directly around the disputed boundary - page 567 opens '## 14.6.2' (a 3-component clause at '##') then nests '### 14.6.2.1', '### 14.6.2.2', '### 14.6.2.3', '#### 14.6.2.3.1'; page 568 opens with 14.6.2.3.2, which therefore resets to '##'; page 569 opens '## 14.6.2.4' then '## 14.6.3'. 14.6.2.3.2 is at '##' for precisely one reason: it is the first heading after a page break. Sampling confirms the model document-wide - page 300 opens '## 11.7.4' then '## 11.8' / '### 11.8.1'; page 301 re-opens '## 11.8' / '### 11.8.1'; pages 700 and 701 both open '## 14.9.26' / '### 14.9.26.1'. The whole-file histogram makes it unarguable: 2304 '##' vs 1413 '###' vs only 96 '####', in a standard containing thousands of 4- and 5-component clauses. The same clause number even appears at two different levels in different page contexts ('## 14.6.13.1.1' at line 24107 and '#### 14.6.13.1.1' at line 24148). (4) The stated harm does not follow. The premise is that markdown heading depth encodes clause depth, so a wrong level relocates a clause in the outline. That premise is false for this document at every point, not just here - '## 14.6', '## 14.6.2', '## 14.6.2.4', '## 14.6.3', '## 14.6.9.4' and '## 14.6.13.1' are all already '##'. A consumer inferring hierarchy from '#' counts would misplace roughly half the standard; a consumer reading the clause number or the section anchor - the only reliable route, and the one the repo's spec-lookup path uses - lands correctly on 14.6.2.3.2 and 14.6.2.3.3. The claim's factual observations about both sources are accurate (the PDF headings are printed as stated; the markdown levels are as quoted). What fails is the classification and the significance: nothing is missing, no content or meaning differs, and the level reset is a uniform artifact of page-boundary handling. Flagging it here would require flagging it on well over a thousand other pages identically.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a page-568 discrepancy. Both headings, their clause numbers, their titles, their section anchors, and the entire body text of the page are transcribed completely and accurately. The only difference is markdown heading DEPTH ('##' vs '####'), which is an artifact of the transcription's page-local heading model - the first clause heading on every page is emitted at '##' and deeper subclauses nest beneath it - triggered here solely because 14.6.2.3.2 begins page 568. The model is document-wide (2304 '##' vs 96 '####'; identical resets observed at pages 300/301, 569, 700/701; clause 14.6.13.1.1 itself appears at both '##' and '####'), so markdown heading depth is not a hierarchy signal anywhere in this file and no content or normative meaning is affected. If the inconsistent nesting is judged worth correcting, it is a single global normalization pass over specs/ISO_COBOL.md keyed on clause-number component count - a transcription-pipeline enhancement, not a per-page reconciliation finding.
